6.216.m: Nārada said: / From that Madhuvana, O king, this Badarikāśrama / is situated at an area of eleven bows' distance.
I shall describe before you the greatly wondrous majesty / of this best of sacred sites, hearing which one is freed from fear.
There was in Magadha, O king, a certain brāhmaṇa named Devadāsa, / truthful, self-restrained, like Dharma himself in visible form,
Accomplished in all branches of learning, like another Bṛhaspati, / pleasing Hari through devotion, like Prahlāda, the king of the Daityas,
Though married, he conquered passion like Pārvatī's beloved [Śiva]; / he was ever devoted to good conduct like the sage Viśvāmitra.
He was respected in the house of the king of Magadha as Droṇa in the Kuru court; / he was generous toward worthy recipients like Bali, lord of the Daityas.
His wife, named Uttamā, was preeminent in virtues like Lakṣmī, / devoted to serving her husband like the daughter of Janaka.
He had an intelligent son, O king, named Aṅgada, / and a daughter named Valayā endowed with auspicious marks.
Of the two, the son was the elder, and the daughter, O king, was younger than him; / that best of the twice-born performed the marriage of both in proper order.
And when that maiden was married, she went to her father-in-law's house, / endowed with auspicious marks, after some time, O king.
Aṅgada, however, of great intellect, bore the burden of the household / like his father, knowledgeable in all scriptures, adorned with the beauty of youth.
Once that best of brahmins, recognizing his son to be capable / in household duties, O lord of kings, addressed his wife:
Devadāsa said: / Listen to my words, O virtuous lady, appropriate at this time; / then let whatever is proper, O auspicious one, be done without delay.
This old age has arrived and will cause the body to fall, / shaking the limbs just like a gale [shakes down] ripe fruit.
It will surely make the brilliance even of the eyes grow dim, / just like the morning hour dims the stars and the moon, O lady of good vows.
This old age will make the gait of the feet faltering and slow / with every single step, like an iron chain.
Therefore, O auspicious woman, so long as this old age does not become fully mature, / that which pertains to the soul must swiftly be done by both of us.
House, son, friend, brother, and parents are indeed perishable, / as are possessions and the like, O lovely one; the wise man should not become attached to them.
Therefore, wandering among all the holy places with senses subdued, / in accordance with the rule of the forest hermit, I shall behold the Lord Hari.
Then, having taken renunciation at some auspicious, supreme holy place, / at the end of karmas that have begun to bear fruit, I will cast off my physical body.
If I am thus freed from vital breath, liberation will ensue, there is no doubt about this, / for my mind is thoroughly fixed upon the lotus feet of the Lord of Śrī.
uttamā said: / What man or what woman would take delight in this perishable / cycle of worldly existence, devoid of consciousness, forsaking Mādhava, the eternal refuge?
Therefore, O lord of my life, take me as well, who serve your lotus feet, / in your company, and quickly cross over the ocean of worldly existence.
This splendid son Aṅgada has become capable of bearing / the burden of the household, and this daughter-in-law is auspicious, his helpmate.
When a son is capable, that foolish man or woman / who does not develop detachment is a fool deceived of spiritual welfare.
Nārada said: / Having thus conferred with one another in secret at that time, / the husband and wife called their son Aṅgada and said this:
The husband and wife said: / Know us, O Aṅgada, as having limbs slackened by the arrival of old age; / we shall strive for our spiritual welfare somewhere upon the holy earth.
The worship of Hari through devotion is declared to be the highest welfare; / for that very purpose, the virtuous on earth strive without selfish desires.
They have no attachment to sense objects, [practice] sameness toward all living beings, / and never have joy or sorrow in pleasure and pain;
they alone are the virtuous in the world who serve the feet of Govinda; / merely by seeing them, a mortal attains fulfillment.
Wandering through holy places, the wise person, eager to see them, / through some dawn of fortune might attain their vision.
Therefore, having placed the burden of the family upon your arms, long as a yoke, / grant us leave, O Aṅgada, to go on pilgrimage to holy places.
If by chance, in the course of pilgrimage to holy places, the sight of a virtuous person / should occur, then, O son, there would be fulfillment for both of us.
Nārada said: / Being thus spoken to by his parents, the son uttered words of approval: / [Aṅgada said:] "This deliverance of the entire family has been declared by you two.
Soon give me your instruction: what may I do that is beneficial to you? / I am ever an obedient servant of your venerable feet.
Take excellent wealth for the sake of giving at holy places, / and take me along also in your company as a servant to serve you."
Nārada said: / Having said this and taken wealth, he went two krośas with them / in their company, and then returned home, having been turned back by them with difficulty.
Those two, having accepted a little wealth, thinking, "May Viṣṇu control us," / subsisting on roots, tubers, and fruits, stayed there for three days.
When the husband and wife set out from there, O lord of the earth, / then on the road a certain great perfected one met them.
Saluted with bent head by both of them, he sat down; / when he had sat down, that king among perfected ones was asked by the two:
"Who are you, whence have you come, and what do you wish to do? Tell us that." / The perfected one said: "I am a perfected one, O best of ascetics; my home is in Kalpagrāma.
I have come from Indraprastha; a great wonder was seen by me there. / There resides the perfected one Kapila, equal to Nārāyaṇa in virtues.
Studying Sāṅkhya from him, I dwell in his hermitage. / Once my glorious guru, Kapila, went forth from his hermitage
to the highly sacred place called Badarī, to bathe in the water of the Yamunā. / There a wild buffalo, afflicted with thirst, in the water of the Yamunā
entered, drank the water, and remembered his previous birth. / Having remembered his previous deeds, that buffalo born of the forest,
emerging swiftly from the water, bowed to the guru Kapila, / and the ascetic spoke in human speech while I was listening, / which I shall relate to you today; listen to this supreme wonder."
The buffalo said: / "O, O portion of Viṣṇu, Kapila, lord of perfected ones, / what is the name of this great holy place? Tell me, who am bowed down.
Verily, by the touch of the water of this supreme holy place, / [the memory] of my previous birth has arisen for me, O highly fortunate one, and also of sinful deeds."
The perfected one said: / Having heard those words of the buffalo, the great sage, / though already knowing that matter, smiled and spoke this:
Kapila said: / "O tiger among buffaloes, who were you in your previous birth? / What deed did you do there, by which you obtained birth as a buffalo?"
The buffalo said: / "Listen, O tiger among sages, to the story of my previous birth. / Formerly, I was a king, the mighty ruler of Kaliṅga.
Deluded by passion, I did not distinguish between my own wife and another's; / I was a plunderer of the wealth of merchants of virtuous conduct, free from sin.

6.216.s:
niśīthenagarerājan gatabhīḥ paryaṭāmyaham
suṃdarībhiḥ parastrībhiḥ krīḍituṃratilīlayā
6.216.d:
निशीथेनगरेराजन् गतभीः पर्यटाम्यहम्
सुंदरीभिः परस्त्रीभिः क्रीडितुंरतिलीलया
6.216.m: At midnight in the city, O king, I would wander without fear / to sport in amorous play with the beautiful wives of others.
In whatever house I saw a beautiful woman, infatuated by passion, / I would dwell there at night like an elephant in the midst of a crop.
Having sported there without hesitation and seized wealth from that house, / I would return again to my own house after some days.
Seated in the midst of the royal assembly by day, I would make two boys of the town / fight before me in vulgar hand-to-hand combat.
Whichever boy wrestled down [his opponent], considering him rich, by force / I would seize his father's wealth, whether small or great, O sage.
He who was defeated there through cowardice, O great sage, / thinking, 'This one does not deserve to remain in my city,' I would kill him.
When even this slaughter began while the king was ruling, / the citizens abandoned the city and went to another region.
Once, O tiger among sages, Durvāsas, wandering the earth, / born of Rudra, Durvāsas came to my city.
Assembling together, all the townsfolk then went to his presence; / bowing down, they spoke this word to him, making known their distress.
The citizens said: / 'O descendant of Atri, tiger among sages, show mercy, O treasure of compassion! / Unite this king, who is devoted to unrighteousness, with righteousness.
Through some dawn of good fortune you have come to us; / save us, like a boat, from the overflowing ocean of sorrow caused by the king!'
"Our wealth was seized by him out of covetousness, O best of sages, / and virtuous women were corrupted by that lustful one without any remorse.
Many children about ten years old were killed. / This king is a storehouse of countless defects, O great sage."
The buffalo said: / "Having thus heard the words of the citizens, the sage, the son of Atri, / thinking, 'He deserves punishment,' then came to me as I sat in the assembly.
Seeing that avadhūta approaching unclothed, / I turned him away through my servants: 'He is not fit to be seen.
His limbs are smeared all over with dust, having the very likeness of a buffalo; / let him be turned away!' Thus I repeatedly ordered those standing near.
Then those servants went swiftly to keep him away. / With merely a roar, the sage turned them all to ashes.
Just as from Sagara [were reduced to ashes the sons] guarding the sacrificial horse of their father, / so, seeing all those servants turned to ashes by his fiery splendor,
I rose up abruptly, intending to flee into the house. / Then that best of sages, addressing me, 'Hey, hey, wicked one!'
cursed me: 'Become a buffalo in the great wilderness now!' / Cursed thus by him, indeed, leaving my royal body then,
I was born as a buffalo in the great wilderness of the Maru country, O sage. / For a long time I lived there, O best of sages.
By what merit I have come here—listen also to that: / Many step-wells, wells, and pools were caused to be dug by me.
The planting of mango and other trees was arranged along the path. / By this merit, O lord, my fall did not happen into hell.
And contact with the water of this sacred place was attained by me. / All this has been related to you—the good and evil of my previous birth,

by which this sacred place was attained by me and this buffalo womb. / Through the touch of the water of this best of sacred places, I became one who remembers his past births. / How may there be liberation from this evil womb? Tell me that, O sage!"
Kapila said: / "This sacred place named Badarī belonging to the Lord of Ramā is of great merit. / Bathe here quickly; surely you will obtain the desire dwelling in your heart."
The siddha said: / Hearing this speech of that [sage], O great sage, the buffalo / entered into that best of sacred places to bathe, desiring heaven.
When, having bathed out of a desire for heaven, he came out of the water to the bank, / at that very moment Śakra arrived from heaven, mounted upon an elephant.

Indra said: / "O king of Kaliṅga, abandon your buffalo body! / Having regained a celestial form, come together with me to heaven. / You bathed with a desire for heaven, and that abode of the gods has been attained by you."

The siddha said: / Addressed thus by him at that time, abandoning the buffalo body / and attaining a celestial form, he mounted the king of elephants.

Having mounted the king of elephants and remained in the sky for a moment, / bowing his head to the god, he praised the sage Kapila.
The Kaliṅga [king] said: / "Homage to you, the supreme lord, the cause of absolute knowledge, / the bridge for the Vedic teachings, the enemy of those opposed to them!
From you arose the practice of Sāṃkhya that brings realization of the truth / even to embodied beings whose minds are seized by illusion, O omnipresent one.
Those who, abandoning what is enjoined by the Veda, behave as they wish, O sage, / you punish them, the punishable ones, plunging them among animals and others.
Indra and the other world-protectors are all your officials; / fearing the punisher, they surely conform to your will.
The ancient gods who opposed the religion of the three Vedas, in age after age, / having descended [into the world], were completely destroyed by you.
Whichever enemies of the thirty [gods] were slain by you, O lord who wields the discus, / they, abandoning their body made of darkness, went to Vaikuṇṭha.
Command me, O Lord of the Universe, to go to the abode of the thirty gods, / and favor Śakra, who bows to you, with the nectar of your glances.
By your grace, O Lord of gods, and that of the sacred place named Badarī, O master, / having cast off my tamasic body, I have attained a sattvic one.
Mounting the king of elephants together with Indra, to the abode of the thirty gods / I go according to my desire, O lord, by the compassion of you, the treasure of compassion."
The siddha said: / Having thus praised the lord of gods, Kapila, that king of Kaliṅga, / bowing to his feet, went to the abode of the thirty gods.
"This wonder was seen by me at the hermitage of Badarikā, O brāhmaṇa, / while serving the guru: even the liberation from sin.
There is no sacred place higher than this in the three worlds that grants all ends of life; / go right there together with your wife, if you desire the highest good.
I am going home to bring to [the place] named Badarī, O twice-born one, / my aged father, who is free from longing and desires liberation."
Nārada said: / Having thus proclaimed the greatness of this best of sacred places named Badarī, O king, / that siddha went to his own home.
Then, after some time, that wise twice-born one, wandering among sacred places / along with his wife, arrived at Indraprastha.
With that very body, O king, he led the two of them to his own abode. / That siddha too, having quickly brought his own father from home,

bathed him, who desired liberation, right there in that sacred place. / He too, the aged father of the siddha, was then, by glorious Vāsudeva,

then the lord, praised by the gods, was led to his own house, / this holy place named Badarī situated within Indraprastha.

grants the object desired in the mind of all creatures through bathing. / The holy glorification of it has been described to you, O king bowed in reverence, / hearing which, indeed, a person never falls into a mother's womb.

6.217.m: The king said: / "The glorification of the origin of Badarī has been described to me by you, O virtuous one, / hearing which my mind attains purity, O sage.
This wondrous, supreme glorification named Śakraprastha, / which grants the four aims of life entirely, O tiger among sages—
on earth there is no sacred place higher than this, granting liberation even to animals, / supreme, destroying all sins merely by its sight, O Nārada.
I wish to hear the glorification of this Haridvāra situated within it, O Nārada, / from you who grant satisfaction.
Deliver me, O sage, who am wretched through ignorance, desires, and actions, / by the description of this sacred place situated in Śakraprastha!"
Nārada said: / "Listen, O fortunate one, I shall describe before you / the glorification of Haridvāra, which gives the fruit of the horse sacrifice.
How a certain sinful dog-cooker here attained the celestial state, / that I shall tell you today; listen with a single mind, O lord.
In the sacred realm of Kurukṣetra, a dog-cooker of sinful deeds / renowned as Kāliga indeed lived outside the city.
Deceiving children five or six years of age belonging to the townspeople, / he forcefully took them into the forest and killed them.
Having killed them, that vile man took their silver, like gold, O king, / consisting of ornaments, gems, and the like, which were on their bodies.
He entered the dwellings of virtuous men at night with a desire to take their wealth; / seeing wayfarers with wealth, he killed them in the deserted forest.
Once, on a solar festival day, people from various directions / came to Kurukṣetra, O king, desiring to receive various gifts.
Having bathed there according to the rules during the solar eclipse, O lord of the earth, / and having given gifts in the prescribed manner, the people departed to their own homes.
A certain foremost among the vaiśyas, laden with great wealth, / set out toward his home behind all the other people.
He was a horseman with twenty foot-soldiers marching before him. / Kāliga, that great sinner, followed him for the sake of his wealth.
Having traveled for several stages with him, that lowest of vaiśyas, / that outcaste, found no opportunity to steal his wealth, O king.
He was unable to seize his wealth even by force, / for the vaiśya was accompanied by twenty men, while he was alone.
Arriving here for the sake of the vaiśya’s wealth, O ruler of the earth, / the sinful one entered his camp in the middle of the night to steal the riches.
As the evil-minded one was entering, he was noticed by one / of the vaiśya’s men who was standing his watch.
Seeing him nearby, that watchman, / while lying down, O king, seized him by both feet.
Holding them and waking the other people, that watchman / was struck with a hand by that wicked thief.
Hearing [the noise], the thief fled, but was seized by the other men then; / killing his captor, he quickly ran away again.
By a certain servant carrying a bow, O king, / that vile man, while running, was swiftly struck down from afar with an arrow.
No sooner was he struck by the arrow than he quickly gave up his life. / And the two attendants of the vaiśya were killed by the thief, O king.
Those three mounted splendid aerial vehicles brought by the divine attendants, O lord of the earth, / and standing in the sky, they addressed this to the vaiśya:
Kāliga and the attendants of the vaiśya said: / 'O noble master of the vaiśyas, this sacred ford is unsurpassed! / At Indraprastha, Haridvāra brings auspiciousness even to sinners.
Though we three have met an untimely death, in this excellent sacred ford / we are going to heaven, O vaiśya; now may auspiciousness be yours!'
Glorious Nārada said: / Having spoken thus, they went to heaven, the auspicious abode of those who perform auspicious deeds, / where enjoyable objects are obtained in abundance just as one desires.
Then, when the night had passed, in the morning the foremost of vaiśyas / performed the cremation of the bodies of his two servants and cast their bones [into the water].
While the bones were being thrown into this sacred ford, O lord, / those two servants returned here from heaven and said this to the vaiśya:
The servants said: / 'O noble master of the vaiśyas, from death in this sacred ford on earth, / even sinful creatures attain heaven; of this there is no doubt.
If the bones of a creature who dies on dry land fall into the water / of this sacred ford, O vaiśya, then his abode shall be in Satyaloka.
Since we two died on dry land, by the casting of our bones into the water, / residence in the realm of Brahmā has been obtained until the end of the cosmic age of Brahmā.
The bones of the thief who died on dry land have not fallen into the water; / therefore, O lord of the vaiśyas, he has stayed [only] in the abode of the gods.
Search for his body too, and quickly throw it into this sacred ford, / so that he, best among gods, may also attain our highest state.
Virtuous men must always do good to others; / even a great injury done by the wicked should not be held against them.'
Nārada said: / Having spoken thus, those two fortunate souls departed to the city of Hari / due to the casting of their bones into the water of the sacred ford of Haridvāra.
That fortunate vaiśya searched for the body of the thief / to burn it, but he could not find it, O lord of the earth.
Returning again to that very crest-jewel of all sacred fords, / Haridvāra, O great king, he bathed with this wish:
'Having fathered virtuous sons, and having satisfied / the brāhmaṇas and kin with wealth acquired through dharma, and having worshipped Viṣṇu through service,
may I, meeting death in you alone, go to the abode of Hari! / O king of sacred fords, salutations to you! This must be granted by you.'
With such a desire, O king, that vaiśya bathed at that desire-yielding / holy site, and then, accompanied by all his servants, went to his own home.
Having gone there, that wise man fathered sons on his wife / and satisfied his kin with wealth acquired through dharma.
Having worshipped the Lord of Kamalā with supreme devotion, O king, / he met his death in this sacred ford, whence he attained Vaikuṇṭha.
Thus, indeed, O king, the greatness of the holy site has been described to you, / of the sacred Haridvāra; hear now the fruit of listening to it.
Whatever fruit a person obtains by giving a droṇa of sesame in the month of Māgha, / that fruit he obtains by listening to its glorification.
The fruit obtained by giving gopīcandana clay and by eating from palāśa leaves / in the month of Kārtika, that very fruit comes from merely hearing its greatness.
Whatever fruit arises from keeping a vigil on Prabodhini in the final watch [of the night], O king, / that fruit arises from listening to the greatness of this sacred ford.
There is no sacred ford in the mortal world equal to Haridvāra / situated in Indraprastha, which bestows the fruit of the four aims of life.

Thus ends the two hundred and seventeenth chapter, named the Description of Haridvāra, in the Glorification of Indraprastha, in the Uttarakhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Purāṇa, the collection of fifty-five thousand [verses].

6.218.m: Nārada said: / Listen further, O fortunate one, to the supremely wondrous glorification, / which grants auspiciousness, of the sacred ford Puṣkara situated here.
By the grace of that sacred ford, Viṣṇu, lord of all gods, / being pleased, resided in the home of Puṇḍarīka for one month. / Here his younger brother, though devoted to sin, attained liberation.
Śibi said: / Who was righteous Puṇḍarīka, and what deed was done by him / because of which the blessed Lord was pleased and dwelt for a month in his home?
How did his evil-minded younger brother attain the abode of glorious Hari / by the grace of this sacred ford? Tell me all, O sage!
While listening to its glorification, my satisfaction is never complete.
Nārada said: / In the city of Vidarbha, O king, lived a highly renowned brāhmaṇa named Mālava, / a knower of Brahman, tranquil, learned, and devoted to Viṣṇu.
He sustained gods, sages, ancestors, living beings, and men; / he was not attached to sensory objects, and was free from greed, delusion, and the like.
Once, O fortunate one, when Jupiter entered Leo, / he went to the exceedingly holy Godāvarī to bathe.
In order to make gifts there, he brought ten thousand palas of gold from home. / Going along the road, that righteous man reflected in his mind thus:
Mālava said: / 'Ten thousand palas of gold have been brought by me from home for the purpose of giving. / It must not be given to just anyone; it must be given to a venerable, virtuous man,
to a brāhmaṇa who possesses nothing, who is a worthy recipient and can render no return favor, / who is venerable; what is given in the proper place and time becomes imperishable.
Having given to Durvāsas what was gathered by gleaning ears of grain, the sage / living by gleaning grain, righteous in soul, abandoned his self and went to the supreme abode.
King Bali, lord of the Dānavas, knowing Vāmana to be a worthy recipient, / gave to him, even though he was an adversary, the three worlds won by his own arms.
Therefore, wealth acquired through dharma must be given by me to a worthy recipient, / solely for the pleasure of Govinda; one should not desire its reward.
My sister's son, the righteous Puṇḍarīka, the crest-jewel of all worthy recipients, / will come from Gajavāhaya, summoned by me.'
"Half of the wealth brought I shall give to that worthy recipient, my sister's son, / but the remainder to learned brāhmaṇas according to rule."
Nārada said: / Having reflected thus, O king, that righteous best of twice-born men, Mālava, / reached the holy Godāvarī after a few days.
His sister's righteous son, Puṇḍarīka, met him; / he had indeed arrived before Mālava, O lord of the earth.
Having bathed there according to rule on the day of the sun's entry into Leo, / he gave half of the wealth to Puṇḍarīka, [saying,] "May Hari be pleased with me."
The righteous Puṇḍarīka also, having bathed in the water of the Godāvarī, / gladly gave a fourth part of his wealth to learned brāhmaṇas.
Having bathed there according to rule and given gifts according to his capacity, / O king, he spoke thus to his sister's son as he was departing for his own home:
Mālava said: / "Salutation is to be spoken to elders, and a blessing to the younger. / Indeed, this meeting of ours has been fleeting.
Such indeed is the union of all living beings with their sons, wives, and the rest. / Therefore, that wise man who from this world of fleeting union
becomes detached, will certainly become a vessel of Hari's grace. / By the grace of Śrī Hari, a living creature becomes devoted to the company of the good.
From that arises the desire to hear Hari's divine play; / and having heard the divine plays of Hari recounted by the good, he himself
praises them with great longing, and then remembers [them] continuously. / From that arises love for the service of Govinda's feet.

Thereby a man quickly crosses the great ocean [of worldly existence], as if by a boat. / For this purpose, O righteous one, striving is made by the good, the wise, and the performers of rites; you too be one who strives."
Nārada said: / Having spoken thus, that man of Vidarbha with difficulty dismissed his sister's son / and, with a tearful face and eyes clouded with tears, went away.
The righteous Puṇḍarīka also set out toward his own house; / after some days, O king, he arrived here at this auspicious place.
He beheld his younger brother named Bharata fallen on the ground, / breathing, smeared with blood flowing from wounds.
Weeping aloud, he asked: "Brother, by whom have you been brought to such a state, / or for what reason did you come here from home?"
While Puṇḍarīka was thus asking, O best of kings, Bharata, afflicted instantly by great pain, surrendered his life-breaths.
Then a wondrous celestial chariot with an entourage descended / from the sky, O king, while people and his elder looked on.
Having mounted it, with a divine body, Bharata, even though an evildoer, / bowing down, spoke this word to his eldest brother:
Bharata said: / "O Puṇḍarīka of great intelligence, by the grace of this holy place Puṣkara, / residence in heaven has been attained by me, sinner though I am.
Although you know my cruel deeds, O brother, / nevertheless I shall tell you today a little that is unknown to you:
How I sported with the courtesan Prabhāvatī, / and how much wealth of that house was spent for the sake of liquor;
and what was lost in gambling, and what was acquired by thievery; / and how on Śivarātri the leftover offering of Śambhu was eaten by me;
and for whose sake a brāhmaṇa named Jebu was defamed by you. / All this deed done by me was known to you, O Puṇḍarīka.
What I did, O brother, when you went to the Godāvarī / is not known to you; I shall tell even that—alas!
When a fortnight had passed after you had set out, / I heard from people a report intolerable to Hari:
'Puṇḍarīka has been invited by his maternal uncle to be given wealth.' / 'Having killed my own uterine brother, Puṇḍarīka, what was brought by him,
the abundant wealth bestowed by Mālava, I will seize. / With that great wealth I will satisfy Prabhāvatī,
and I will gamble at will with those who know the dice.' / Having considered thus, blocking your path, I stayed here,
intending to kill you and take the abundant wealth, O highly intelligent one. / When the wealth had passed by, O brother, a merchant caravan arrived from somewhere.
I slept here at night, O highly intelligent one, among those merchants. / Then in the middle of the night, a thief entered there to steal
the merchants' wealth in that caravan crowded with people. / When that thief fled having taken some wealth, / the servants at once ran after him, shouting loudly.
The servants said: / 'Seize him! Seize him! This thief is fleeing swiftly, / having stolen abundant wealth from the midst of many of us!'
Bharata said: / Hearing their words, O brother, with a desire to seize it, / I immediately ran ahead after him in order to take it.
Then those servants of the merchants, thinking me to be his protector, / all struck violently with swords in hand, bearing blades.
Among them, a best of twice-born men, saying 'I am a brāhmaṇa,' / was struck down with a sharp-edged sword by me, a wretched sinner.
And I was struck by those servants of the merchants wielding swords. / In the morning, those merchants departed for the country of their destination.
Then you arrived here and saw me gasping for breath, / my body smeared with flowing blood, unconscious with pain and delusion.

Thus has this been told, brother: the purpose for which I came, / and how I met an untimely death—that too has been told by me.

Thus ends the two hundred and eighteenth chapter, in the Glorification of the Kālindī, in the Uttarakhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Purāṇa, the collection of fifty-five thousand [verses].

6.219.m:
The two hundred and nineteenth chapter.
Nārada said: / Having heard his words, the noble-minded Puṇḍarīka / spoke to that relative of his, as his own companions listened:
Puṇḍarīka said: / "By what merit did your death take place in this holy place, Bharata? / If you know, tell me; for your sin is widely known."
Bharata said: / "Listen to this, Puṇḍarīka; I will tell you before you / the merit yielding this holy place that was performed in this birth.
Once, returning to my house after winning wealth, / I saw in the market the dead body of a dead, helpless child.
Placing it on my head and carrying it to the auspicious bank of the Gaṅgā, / having adorned it with clothes and other items, I performed the funeral rites such as cremation.
All that wealth acquired through gambling was spent by me; / by that merit, this auspicious holy place was attained by me.
Do perform the funerary rites for my body, beginning with cremation."

Śrī Nārada said: / When the funerary rites were performed, O king, Bharata, although sinful, / went to heaven by the grace of this holy place, Puṣkara. / How Viṣṇu, Hari, for one month in the house of Puṇḍarīka

dwelt by the grace of this holy place—hear that now! / In this holy place, that righteous one, having seen even Bharata's good destination, / thought in his heart: 'This holy place truly grants desires.'
With this longing, that learned Puṇḍarīka bathed here: / 'May Hari in his own form dwell in my house during the month of Māgha.'
Having bathed thus with a desire in this holy place that grants all goals, O best of kings, / Puṇḍarīka departed for his own home.
He related the death of his brother Bharata to their kinsmen; / and they too, hearing it, made lamentation, their minds obscured by delusion.
Then Puṇḍarīka, performing his daily duties in his own house, / dwelt in great bliss, thinking, "Hari will come for austerities."
Then, on the full moon day of the month of Pauṣa, he held a great festival, / thinking, "Tomorrow Hari will surely come to my house."
By sprinkling sandalwood water and plastering with cow dung, / and with fourfold patterns of pearl powder, he decorated his dwelling.
He fed two hundred brāhmaṇas with various types of food, / and he satisfied them with abundant priestly gifts.
With singers skilled in various instruments and possessed of melodious voices, / he kept a vigil at night, singing along with his own kin.
Then, at dawn, having dismissed all those singers and others, / he sat inside the house, yearning for the arrival of Govinda.
Then, sending back his mount near his house, / [Hari] entered the interior of the house to fulfill the desire of his devotee.
Seeing that Mādhava had arrived, O king, / Puṇḍarīka quickly rose from his seat and bowed with his head.
And that righteous man, overjoyed at the sight of Govinda, / worshipped him with the offering of water for guest-reception and the rest, and seated him on a chair, and spoke:
Puṇḍarīka said: / That which destroys worldly existence has been clearly performed by you. / Therefore, O Viṣṇu, you who maintain the world, stay here
until the completion of this holy austerity. / Where you and your servants dwell in mutual service,
right there indeed is Vaikuṇṭha, free from all blemishes. / In whichever house your deeds are described by the virtuous, O Lord,
there Hari resides, facing them—so it has been heard by us. / They in whose words is your name, in whose heart is your handsome form,
and in whose ears is the attributing of your qualities—they alone are the truly virtuous. / O Lord, your heart is inclined toward the service of those
upon whose heads rests the offering of flowers dedicated to you—they alone are the truly virtuous. / Those whose intellect is impartial toward enemy and friend, O Lord of Kamalā,
and toward increase and loss—they alone are the truly virtuous. / Those whose minds are not agitated even when there is cause for agitation,

they alone indeed are the virtuous, O Lord of Lakṣmī. / Where you are, there are the virtuous; where the virtuous are, there are you. / Therefore, recognize me as virtuous, and dwell in my house during Māgha.
Nārada said: / Hearing this speech of Puṇḍarīka, Mādhava / spoke words, illuminating the quarters with the radiance of his teeth.
The Blessed Lord said: / You are the best among the virtuous on earth, O noble-minded one, / since you bathed at the sacred ford with the desire for my company.
Rise, O twice-born, take a bath in the waters of the Jāhnavī in the month of Māgha; / at the end of Māgha, on the full moon day, I will make you bathe at Puṣkara.
Whatever full fruit is born of bathing at Prayāga in the month of Māgha, / all that is obtained by a single day's bath at the sacred ford of Puṣkara.
Nārada said: / Being thus addressed by Murāri, that best of brāhmaṇas, Puṇḍarīka, / bathed in the waters of the Gaṅgā just as the sun rose slightly.
Puṇḍarīka worshipped the visibly manifest Lotus-eyed One / with tulasī, blooming flowers, barley grains, saffron, and sandalwood.
Having perfumed the limbs of the Lord of Ramā with incense of agallochum, / he waved before him five lamps with camphor.
Having fed the teacher of the world with the four kinds of food, / he fanned him with chowries as he slept on a jeweled couch.
At times he massaged the feet of that Lord of Ramā; / he gave him betel rolls combined with camphor.
At times that best of brāhmaṇas stood before the Lord of Śrī, / holding a mirror in his hand while he tied his turban.
In this way, offering service to the One who cuts through worldly existence as he resided in his home, / the brāhmaṇa spent the entire month of Māgha.
Then, at the close of Māgha on the full moon day, he saw / Tārkṣya standing before the Lord of Ramā, having arrived at the mere thought of him.
Seeing him, the Lotus-eyed One said to Puṇḍarīka: / The Blessed Lord said: Hear, O best of the twice-born, the word I speak to you.
For your bathing at the sacred ford of Puṣkara situated at Indraprastha, / according to your wish, I have given that I have dwelt [here] for a month.
Today, mounting the king of birds together with me, O noble-minded one, / go to that crest-jewel of holy places, that very Pratipuṣkara.
Bathing in that [ford] which grants the four aims of life, whatever you desire, / that I shall give you, because I am under your control, O twice-born.
Even your sinful brother Bharata, having died there, went / to heaven, desiring the pleasures of heaven; what more can be said of it?
Nārada said: / Having spoken thus, that lord of the gods, having mounted that best of brāhmaṇas upon the king of birds, O king, / went to the lord of all sacred places.
By him, along with that vital breath, a light emerged / from Puṇḍarīka's body and entered the abode of Govinda.
In this way, O king, by bathing at this sacred ford of Puṣkara situated at Indraprastha, / Puṇḍarīka attained union with the Lord.
Thus, on account of that sacred ford, Govinda too / lived happily in his house for a month like his own kinsman, O king.
By whom can the greatness of Puṣkara be described? / Only a ten-millionth part of this [place] located at Śakraprastha has been described by me.
By hearing this glorification with faith, or even by reciting it, / a person obtains the fruit of a horse sacrifice, O lord of the earth.

6.219-2.m: Nārada said: / Before you I shall describe with faith the supremely holy greatness / of Prayāga, the king of sacred places, belonging to Śiva.
Viśvāvasu, a gandharva renowned throughout the world, O protector of the earth, / once went to the assembly of Brahmā on Mount Sumeru to sing.
There Viśvāvasu beheld the best of gods seated upon an excellent throne, / attended by hosts of gods, O protector of the earth.
Near the seat of Brahmā, seated upon an excellent throne, O king, / he beheld Indraprastha like a second lord of the world.
He saw the king of sacred places waving a chowrie over the heads / of the king of gods and the two, Brahmā and Indraprastha, O king.
Other sacred places of the gods were seen by him standing / at a distance from the two, O lord of the earth, with hands folded in reverent salutation.
Before the two, he sang an excellent gandharva melody, O king; / and leaving the gods, he went to Satyaloka along with the sacred places.
Then the wise Viśvāvasu, seeing the magnificence of the sacred place / of Indraprastha, O best of kings, said to Hāhā:
Viśvāvasu said: / O tiger among gandharvas, this sacred ford named Indraprastha / is exceedingly wonderful among the multitudes of sacred places in this world,
in that it occupied an equal seat situated near the seat / of Brahmā, the guru of the mobile and immobile, whose lotus feet are worshipped by gods!
Even the king of sacred places, standing behind it, [waves] a chowrie over its head, / and has now become like a servant; what need be said of other holy places?
The holy places that exist on the earth grant the fruit of the three aims of life; / but this sacred ford of Indraprastha grants the fruit of all four aims of life.
The sacred places situated here are certainly of such a kind in their qualities / that even by Śeṣa their great virtues cannot be praised.
Nārada said: / Having thus seen the majesty of Indraprastha, the wise Viśvāvasu / went to his home, O king, which was purifying and granted all desires.
Just as Śakra, the husband of Śacī, is supreme among all the gods, / and Brahmā [surpasses] him, so this Prayāga is superior among sacred places.
Even superior to that, O great king, is this Śakraprastha; / this Prayāga, O king, is seen to be contained within it.
I shall narrate what happened here in the case of the courtesan Mohinī. / On the bank of the Narmadā river is the city of Māhiṣmatī, O king.
There lived a prostitute named Mohinī, endowed with abundant wealth, / endowed with beauty and youth, and accomplished in dance and song.
Greedy for wealth, she committed many sins: / seven murders of Brahmins were committed, and many female servants were killed.
And their pregnancies were aborted many times by that sinful woman; / thus her prime youth was spent by her in sinful deeds.
Then, after some time, old age came upon her body; / her body gripped by old age, her longing for sensual objects ceased.
She paid no heed to young men, nor did they [heed] her, O lord of the earth; / she did not trust anyone with her wealth, earned through sin.
She did not give it away, nor enjoy it herself, nor deposit it anywhere. / Once, waking up in the middle of the night, she reflected thus:
“When I am dead, to whom will this wealth belong, acquired through sins? / That [sin] will lead me to terrible, utterly dreadful hell.
The female servants and their husbands will enjoy that wealth of mine; / why should I not myself now secure a good destination with it?”
Having thought thus, turning her mind fully toward dharma, / she constructed pleasure gardens, lakes, stepped wells, ordinary wells, and temples of the gods.
All around the city she set up water-stations for travelers; / and during the hot season, O great king, she gave food to them.
Near her home she built a rest-house for the stay of travelers from afar, / and to them she continually gave excellent food.
Thus engaged in dharma, O king, that Mohinī / became afflicted with fever in the course of time, and she thought to herself:
“Even though vast wealth has indeed been spent by me for the sake of dharma, / nevertheless there is still abundant gold, silver, and other valuables remaining.
I shall knowingly give this to those learned in the Vedas,” she thought. / Having so decided, the twice-born of the city were summoned by Mohinī.
They did not come, O protector of the earth, knowing it to be a dreadful acceptance of gifts. / Then she divided her own wealth into two portions:
one portion was given to the female servants, and the other to travelers from afar; / she herself, O king, that Mohinī, became destitute.
Knowing that death had arrived close at hand, / the female servants abandoned her, took the wealth, and went wherever they wished,
Thinking thus: 'When indeed she becomes freed from the fever, / then she will certainly take back that wealth which was given.'
Then, O protector of the earth, having fasted eighteen times, / by the remaining span of her life she was freed from the fever.
She had a female friend named Jaradgavā, O protector of the earth; / she promptly attended upon her with wholesome food and remedies, untiringly.
After some days, she became fully nourished again; / yet she ate in the house of that Jaradgavā with feelings of shame:
“I lived here in comfort; today misery has arrived; / because of poverty I must not remain,” she thought, and departed elsewhere.
As she went through the forest, O king, Mohinī was struck down by city thieves, / who thought: “She is leaving with wealth.”
Finding no wealth on her person, / she was abandoned still breathing by the city thieves in that very forest, O king.
Then a certain Vaikhānasa hermit, carrying the water of this Prayāga / in his water-pot, O king, arrived in this forest.
Seeing her fallen, her body wounded by weapons, / begging for water with a gesture of her hand, O king,
the Vaikhānasa said: / “Who are you? By whom has your body been wounded with sharp weapons? / Or why have you come alone to this uninhabited forest?
This is the auspicious water of the Prayāga situated at Indraprastha; / it has been brought through the rise of some good fortune, desiring your well-being.”
Thus addressed by him, she, unable to speak, opened her mouth / to drink that water, with the desire: 'May I become the chief queen.'
Then, when the water of this Prayāga was poured into her mouth, / that courtesan Mohinī gave up her life, O king.
At the moment of her life-breath’s departure, she had desired queenship; / therefore, she became the queen of Vīravarman in the Drāviḍa country,
having taken birth in the house of the king of Kerala, because of drinking the holy water, / [a king] endowed with noble lineage, virtuous conduct, wealth, and sovereignty, O protector of the earth.
Then the lotus-eyed girl possessed a body as fair as gold; / therefore, her father gave her the name Hemāṅgī.
Once, Hemāṅgī, adorned with golden ornaments, / went to the house of her friend Kalā, the minister’s daughter.
There she was bathed with lacquer-scented oil and fed / with various foods, O king, and was seated upon an excellent seat.
Her braided hair interwoven with flowers, adorned in fine silk, / holding a roll of betel in her mouth, she spoke to Kalā.

Hemāṅgī said: / “O Kalā, heed my words, you who speak sweetly like a cuckoo: / show me whatever wonderful object there is in your house.”

Thus ends the two hundred and twentieth chapter, named the Description of Indraprastha, in the Glorification of the Kālindī, in the Uttarakhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Purāṇa, the collection of fifty-five thousand [verses].

The two hundred and twenty-first chapter.
Nārada said: / Thus addressed by that king's wife, O king, Kalā / had a golden casket brought from her own treasury and placed before her.

and said, O great king: “O queen, inside this is a great, wonderful / book, O lady; in it are many pictures indeed.

Opening it, let it be seen a little, whatever there is in this book; / your mind will surely delight in looking at the illustrations contained therein.”

Having said this, that wife of the king had the female servant open the casket, / and with her hand she took the book lying within it.

There she beheld the incarnations in brief; / first, then, the terrestrial globe of fifty crores of yojanas.

There a golden earth was seen, endowed with darkness and endowed with moisture; / between the two, O king, was Mount Lokāloka.

Then having seen the seven continents surrounded by seven oceans, / the rivers, mountains, and regions in these, O highly wise one,

that beloved of the king, beholding this continent of Bhārata, / looked upon the rivers, foremost among which were the Yamunā and the Jāhnavī.

6.219-2.m:
This auspicious Indraprastha situated on the bank of the Yamunā, / the sacred place together with Vraja, that fortunate lady saw, O king.

Having seen here this sacred Prayāga fashioned by Brahmā, / that intelligent woman remembered the deeds performed in her previous birth.

Then, rising in silence, she quickly went to her own palace, / having resolved thus: “I shall not eat; I shall depart from here to the sacred place.”

Right then, Hemāṅgī, the devoted wife, / wishing to go together with her beloved, said this to Vīravarman, [regarding] the king of sacred places:

Hemāṅgī said:
O lord of my life, listen to my words which bestow dharma.
And act upon them, O fortunate one; your desire will soon be fulfilled.

Formerly I was a courtesan named Mohinī, who committed many sins.
In my youth and in old age, a slight inclination toward dharma arose in my mind.

The wealth acquired through sin was spent by me on dharma.
When, having become penniless, O king, I set out from my city,

then, as I was going into a deserted forest, thieves struck me,
wretched, distressed by poverty, and sinful, in their desire to seize wealth.

With my limbs wounded by sharp weapons, gasping for breath, unconscious,
the thieves, their desires frustrated, abandoned me there and left.

Then an ascetic, carrying the water of Prayāga,
went to Indraprastha and arrived there in that very forest.

Seeing me fallen there in that condition, that ascetic asked:
"Who are you? From where do you come? Why, and by whom have you been struck?"

Then nothing was spoken by me; only that sacred water was requested.
He poured it into my mouth, and then I cast off my body.

At the moment of my life's departure, hearing that that water fulfills all desires,
I wished, O lord: "May I become a queen!"

By the grace of that sacred water, O king, an ocean of supreme conduct and good character,
I became the mistress of your household, born into a good family.

Now I wish to see, O king, together with you,
that Prayāga, the desire-granting king of sacred places situated in Indraprastha.

When I set out towards the king of sacred places, O king, O lord,
only then will I eat food; such is the vow made by me.

The king said:
How am I to know this that you have spoken, O tremulous-eyed one?
Give me proof, O auspicious lady, and I will do as you have said.

Nārada said:
When this was said by the king, a voice arose in the sky at that time.
The voice from the sky said:
"A true word was spoken, O king, by this wife of yours.

In the sacred Prayāga, best of sacred places, situated at Indraprastha—
having gone there, bathe, and you will obtain whatever you desire."

Nārada said:
Hearing that voice originating in the sky, the king
fell like a staff upon the ground, saying: "I bow to the one who speaks this."

Then, having summoned his minister and entrusted the kingdom to him,
he mounted a chariot with her and set out for that foremost sacred place.

In a few days he arrived there together with Hemāṅgī.
The king, accompanied by his wife, offered milk at the king of sacred places.

The husband and wife both bathed there in that auspicious, desire-fulfilling sacred place:
"May attainment of Vaikuṇṭha with this body come to me through Prayāga!"

With that longing, the moment the couple bathed there, O ruler of the earth,
the two foremost gods arrived, riding upon a goose and the king of birds.

Beholding those two who had arrived, King Vīravarman,
bowing with his head, praised the two gods with concentrated mind.

The king said: / Homage to you both, O tigers among gods, who possess dark and red / bodies, silken garments, and the luster of gold and vermilion.

I praise you two, in whom purity and passion are prominent, the causes of the preservation and creation of the moving and unmoving,
lords of the wondrous realms of Vaikuṇṭha and Satya, possessing four and two arms, riding the king of birds [and the goose].

You who bestow true liberation and worldly enjoyment upon people endowed with dispassion or attachment,
whose lotus feet are praised by the gods—with my head bowed in pure devotion I pay homage.

O Govinda, whose feet are praised by the gods, no one knows your true nature,
because you are beyond primordial matter and the soul, far beyond the reach of mind and speech.

Blessed in this world is that man, O Supreme Self, who, considering this universe to be momentary,
worships with undivided mind your lotus feet, which are praised by hosts of sages.

Service to your feet and this sacred place are difficult to attain,
bestowing the fruit of desired objectives upon men who worship.

Even so, this pair should be served for liberation, not for the attainment of anything else;
he who serves with any other desire is indeed deceived.

The virtuous, wishing to overcome, having worshipped you and this sacred place that bestows liberation,
desire nothing else, transcending all the worlds.

Nārada said:
Having thus praised the Lord of gods and the Lord of the world, when that ruler of the earth stood silent,
then, O king, that Hemāṅgī spoke:

"O Lord of Padmā, with eyes like lotus petals! O Brahmā, seated on the dreadful seat, teacher of Bhāratī!
Homage to both of you! If you are pleased with this wretched mind, deliver me from the ocean of worldly existence.

By the grace of this sacred place, O lord, I became a queen;
the sight of both of you, difficult even for the gods to attain, has been obtained.

You two know the minds of all; grant the desire of our hearts,
which was formed by both of us at the time of bathing for the supreme goal."

Thus praised by both of them, those two foremost gods,
with gracious faces, addressed the husband and wife:

Hari and Brahmā said:
Blessed are you, O Hemāṅgī, since your husband has been delivered by you;
though his mind was attached to royal pleasures, he has been delivered through association with this [place].

For kings attached to worldly objects, such liberation as your husband has obtained
by the grace of this sacred place is hard to attain.

Nārada said:
Having said this and looked upon Garuḍa, the foremost of birds,
those two best of gods went to the Satyaloka, O ruler of men.

There they were all worshipped by Brahmā according to rule, O king;
out of regard for his mind, they stayed for a single muhūrta.

Then Hari, mounting Garuḍa together with both of them, the husband and wife,
went to glorious Vaikuṇṭha, O king.

Thus has this majesty of the king of holy bathing-places been told to you, / which is holy, destroys all sins, confers fame, and grants sons, O king.

Whatever human being constantly hears this or recites it
shall go to his desired realm; this which has been spoken by me is true.

6.220.m:
Nārada said:
Listen, O King Śibi; I will describe before you
the sacred, renowned, life-giving, supreme glorification of Kāśī.

At Kāśī, situated on the bank of Indraprastha, there was a certain tree
named the śiṃśapā, O king, in the ancient, holy Kṛta age.

There was a certain crow there, who had built a nest in that tree;
beneath it, a great serpent lived in a hollow.

Once the crow's mate, having left two eggs in the nest,
went somewhere and did not return to her nest.

That crow, personally protecting the pair of eggs,
remained high up on that very śiṃśapā tree, O ruler of the earth.

Then once at midnight a great whirlwind arrived;
it snapped the śiṃśapā tree, O king, even from its firm root.

As the śiṃśapā was brought down by the whirlwind, underneath it
the crow and the serpent were crushed and lost their lives.

Those three—the śiṃśapā, the crow, and the serpent—assuming divine bodies,
mounted three celestial chariots and went to the abode of the Lord of Śrī.

Śibi said:
O divine sage, by what merit was the city that grants liberation attained by them?
Who were those three formerly? Tell me everything, O Nārada!

Nārada said:
There was a brāhmaṇa from the Kurujāṅgala region named Śravaṇa; / his wife was named Kuṇḍā, and his brother was Kuraṇṭaka.
He constantly ate without having bathed, a glutton who enjoyed sweet foods in secret; / because of that fault, Śravaṇa became a village crow.
His brother Kuraṇṭaka, however, was an extreme unbeliever, / an uprooter of the path of Śruti and Smṛti, and a reviler of the gods.
Because of that fault, when he died he became a black snake; / and that Kuṇḍā, Śravaṇa's wife, shared in both their faults.
Therefore, having attained the state of an immovable plant, she gave shelter to both of them. / Thus has that conduct in their previous birth been recounted to you, O king.
Hereafter I shall proclaim their merit, by which the three of them / reached that lovely city Kāśī, presided over by Viśveśvara, O king.
Once, returning to their own home from another village, / they saw a milch-cow belonging to some traveler submerged in a well,
and, without being prompted by him, they rescued her. / Hearing what was related by the two of them, Kuṇḍā said, “Well done!”
By virtue of that merit, the three of them attained a rare death, / and from Kāśī, situated on the bank at Indraprastha, they ascended to Vaikuṇṭha.
Although this Kāśī is the city of the Great Lord, O king, / nevertheless a creature who dies in it rejoices in Hari's Vaikuṇṭha.
Thus has the supreme glorification of Kāśī been related to you, O king. / What else do you desire to hear? Tell that to me.

Śibi said:
O sage, you have mentioned three holy places of the Great Lord: / Kāśī, Śivakāñcī, and likewise another, Gokakarṇa.
The greatness of one, Kāśī, has been proclaimed by you, O great sage; / let that of Gokakarṇa and Śivakāñcī also be told, if there is any.

Nārada said:
Gokakarṇa is an exclusively Śaiva holy place, supremely purifying; / a man who dies there, O king, becomes Śiva—there is no doubt of this.
If a creature should die there on land, in water, or in the air, / then, becoming Śiva, he disports upon the peak of Kailāsa.
For one who has died here at the sacred site of Gokakarṇa there is no rebirth; / together with Śiva, O king, he attains liberation forever.
I shall describe to you also the glorification of this Gokakarṇa, O intelligent one, / which was heard by me from the mouth of Brahmā, O lord.
One gavyūti from Prayāga, close to Gurukṣetra, / there is that Maryādā mountain, seen to be of auspicious sight.
There was a very cruel Bhilla named Karkaṭa; / his wife was named Jarā, and she had slain five husbands.
Then that Jarā prepared a sweetmeat mixed with poison / to kill the sixth, Karkaṭa. Then he heard [of it] from his sister.
From the mouth of his own [sister], O king, that noble Bhilla / Karkaṭa, exceedingly fierce, set out to kill that woman.
When that Bhilla chief went, sword in hand, to slay her, / as soon as she knew the attempt to kill her, she fled.
Frightened, she ran to the forest, desiring to preserve her own life, / as she was pursued by that Karkaṭa, O king.
Here at the sacred site of Gokakarṇa, seized by him, sword in hand, / her head was severed with a sword, and her body was thrown into the water
of that Gokakarṇa sacred site, while he returned to his own place. / Even though sinful, that Jarā, having met her death there at Gokakarṇa,
became a companion of Pārvatī on the peak of Kailāsa, O king. / I have related to you this glory of Gokakarṇa.
Now I shall describe to you the purifying glorification of Śivakāñcī. / In Śivakāñcī also, situated on the bank at Indraprastha, O lord,
that supreme goal is attained by men which was proclaimed by me for Gokakarṇa. / Here the glorious Mahādeva, having propitiated Viṣṇu,
the lord of all gods, attained the status of the king of devotees and essential knowledge. / Therefore all of us, the sons of Brahmā, constantly
worship that Great Lord, desiring genuine devotion and knowledge. / Here, O king, the demon Bāṇa propitiated the Great Lord,
fasting for a hundred years, desiring to become one of his attendants. / Pleased with him, the Blessed Lord granted him his own status as an attendant,
and he himself forever became the guardian of his city. / Formerly, O king, this city belonged to the high-souled Viṣṇu;
it was given to Śiva by Viṣṇu, who was pleased by his austerity. / In this city an event occurred long ago that produces great wonder:
how a brāhmaṇa who was a devotee of Śiva attained Vaikuṇṭha. / There was a virtuous brāhmaṇa, O king, named Heraṃba,
constantly engaged in the worship of Śiva with body, mind, and speech. / Once, that illustrious one, wandering among the sacred sites of Śiva,
a devotee of Śiva, arrived here in Śivakāñcī, pleasing to Śiva, O king. / And that wise man did not leave this charming place.
Afterward, he surrendered his life right there in its waters. / Right there the attendants of glorious Mahādeva took that best of brāhmaṇas
and set out for the immovable Kailāsa by his command. / Then on the way, the attendants of Hari arrived from Vaikuṇṭha;
they endeavored to take that best of the twice-born by force from them. / A great battle ensued among those attendants of Hari and Śarva.
In that battle there was victory for none, nor any defeat. / Then Viṣṇu, seated upon Garuḍa, arrived there from Vaikuṇṭha,
and from Kailāsa came the Great Lord, the upholder of the three worlds, mounted on a bull. / Seeing each other's face and smiling, those two lords of the universe,
watched the great battle fought by the attendants right in the sky. / Then Viṣṇu, restraining his own attendants and the Śaivas fighting in the sky,
placed that twice-born upon Garuḍa and went to Śiva's abode. / Mādhava, accompanied by Śiva, by his attendants, and by his own [attendants],
went along the path, glorious, praised and venerated by the thirty [gods]; / having gone, he entered that mountain, with Mahādeva in front,
showing to that twice-born the delightful beauty of it. / Then from that Kailāsa, having been venerated with supreme devotion
by Mahādeva, Mādhava went at that time to Vaikuṇṭha. / That twice-born too, the illustrious one, by the grace of this holy place,
having obtained the vision of Govinda, rejoiced in the presence of Hara. / Thus has the glory of Śivakāñcī been related to you, O king.
Now listen with full concentration to the name of the seven holy places; / this sacred site, O great king, bestows the fruit of the four aims of life
merely through seeing, touching, meditating, or even remembering, O king. / In this place, great austerities for the sake of creation were performed
by the great sages headed by Vasiṣṭha; they attained forbearance there, O king. / The righteous Marīci also, bathing for the sake of a son,
obtained here that excellent son, the illustrious Kaśyapa. / Atri also here pleased the foremost among gods with austerities,
and obtained from them three sons: Soma, Durvāsas, and Datta. / The righteous Aṅgiras also, by the grace of this holy place,
She obtained sons, and those born in their lineage were the Āṅgirasa brahmins. / Pulaha also obtained a son, Dambholi, most full of virtues.
who formerly became Agastya, O king, by plunging into this very sacred site. / In this very sacred site a son was obtained by Pulastya as he practiced austerities,
the illustrious Kubera, who was a friend of Umā's lord. / Kratu's sons also were born here, the Vālakhilyas by thousands.
By the grace of this holy bath, all of them became celibate ascetics. / Vasiṣṭha too, of great austerities, obtained sons beginning with Raja.
Only seven [such sons], O tiger among kings! Its greatness has been described. / Moreover, there are many other sacred places, O lord of the earth,

Such as the hermitage of Kapila, Kedāra, Prabhāsa, and others, O lord. / Even in millions of years, O king, their greatness / Cannot be told even by the infinite [Śeṣa]; how could it by people like me?

Saubhari said:
Having spoken thus, the best of sages, Nārada, that bull among ascetics, / Went to Śiva's [abode] through the sky, chanting the virtues of Nārāyaṇa.
King Śibi Auśīnara, hearing from the mouth of the sage / The majesty of Śakraprastha, considered himself fulfilled, O king.
Having bathed there duly at Indraprastha, that king, / After performing all proper rites, departed for his own city.
Thus has the glorification of Indraprastha been related to you by me, O lord— / Of the holy place on the bank of the Yamunā that purifies people.
In the Kali age, those devoid of faith will show no regard for this / Indraprastha, O king of kings, the crest-jewel of all sacred places.
Whatever fruit is obtained from listening to the eighteen Purāṇas and the Mahābhārata / Arises from the greatness of this Śakraprastha.
Whatever fruit comes from taking a hundred thousand baths in the month of Māgha at daybreak, / That arises through faith from hearing this greatness.
Whoever listens with faith to its glorification, O protector of the earth, / By him the ancestors, the gods, and likewise the sages are gratified.
Whatever fruit comes through Kṛcchra, Atikṛcchra, Parāka, and Cāndrāyaṇa vows and the like, / That arises from hearing its greatness with faith.
Whatever fruit belongs to all the sacrifices beginning with the horse sacrifice, O lord of the earth, / That arises from hearing its greatness with faith.

Sūta said:
Having thus heard from Saubhari the glorification of Indraprastha, / King Yudhiṣṭhira, O Śaunaka, went to the city of Hastināpura.
Then, having pacified his good brothers and [the Kauravas] led by Duryodhana, / He went to holy Indraprastha with the desire to perform the Rājasūya.
Approaching Govinda, his family deity, who had arrived from Dvārakā, / That lord of the earth sacrificed with the Rājasūya sacrifice.
“This sacred place gives liberation even to one who curses [me]”— / Thinking thus, Hari slew Śiśupāla right there.
Because of dying in that very sacred place on earth, Śiśupāla also / Attained union with Kṛṣṇa, the bestower of all objects of desire.
Where Śiśupāla was slain, and where the sacrifice was performed, / There a very wide pond was fashioned by Bhīma with his mace.
Known as Bhīmakuṇḍa, it became a purifier on earth, / On the southern side of the Kālindī, half a gavyūti away on the earth's surface.
Whatever fruit comes from bathing in the Kālindī situated at Indraprastha, / That same fruit is produced in that pond; there is no doubt about this.

Sūta said:
In whichever holy site a creature resides, in that holy site year after year / He should atone for his transgressions through righteous acts such as circumambulation.
And whatever person circumambulates it every single year / Is not stained by the faults of sins committed against the sacred site.
One who does not perform circumambulation does not attain the perfection of the site; / Therefore, circumambulation should be performed at a holy site by those desiring its fruit.
One who performs the circumambulation chanting the names of Hari / Obtains at every step the fruit born of the gift of a brown cow.
A blessed man who performs the circumambulation of Śakraprastha / On the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight of Caitra is released from all sins.

6.223.m:
Śaunaka said:
O Sūta, O Sūta of great fortune, you are fortunate in the ocean of worldly existence, / In that you cause us, who are deeply immersed in it, to drink an abundance of nectar!
O virtuous one, teach us who desire to cross over existence / The jewel of mantras, pure in essence, of which the moving and unmoving world consists.

Sūta said:
Listen, O Śaunaka; I will tell of the wondrous jewel of mantras / Which was spoken to Dilīpa by the great-souled Vasiṣṭha.
Once Dilīpa, having bowed down just as you have done, / Asked this of his teacher Vasiṣṭha, that tiger among twice-borns.

Dilīpa said:
O venerable one, all duties have been explained by you in detail— / The duties joined with castes and life-stages, the daily and occasional rites,
The duties of kings, sacrifices, pilgrimage sites, gifts, vows, and the like, / Bestowing the enjoyment of imperishable heaven, have been heard by me, O best of sages.
Now I wish to hear the eternal path to liberation, / By which I may happily go [to it]; O Brahman, please tell that.
What mantra of all mantras is the sole remedy for the disease of worldly existence? / Indeed, for all embodied beings, which supreme [mantra] is the bestower of liberation?
Relate that according to reality, out of the weight of your affection for me.

Vasiṣṭha said:
It has been well asked by you, O king, who desire the welfare of all the world; / I will tell the supreme secret, the sole boat to cross over cyclic existence.
In ancient times, all the great sages, devoted to sacrifices and gifts, pure, / Asked Brahmā's son, Nārada, the best of sages:

The great sages said:
O venerable one, by what mantra do we go to the supreme abode? / Tell us that, O fortunate one; you ought to show favour.

Nārada said:
In ancient times, all the yogins, Sanaka and the rest, / In private asked the Grandfather [Brahmā] about the one, very difficult-to-obtain path of liberation.

Brahmā said:
Listen, all you yogins, to this wondrous secret:
All the gods and the ascetics whose wealth is austerity do not know it. / At the beginning of creation, the imperishable god Nārāyaṇa told it to me,
When he was duly worshipped by me together with the goddess, the Supreme Mistress. / Then the imperishable Lord Nārāyaṇa was pleased with me,
And gave me the lordship over creatures, consisting of all speech born of the Veda, / The mantras that are luminous, both pervasive and non-pervasive.
Then I spoke to that god, the ancient Supreme Person: / 'O venerable one, by what mantra is the crossing of cyclic existence for men [achieved]?
Explain that to me according to reality, for the benefit of all the world indeed. / What mantra of all mantras is free from preparatory rites,
Therefore I will tell you the secret by which men may attain me.
Of all mantras it is the jewel of mantras, bringing auspiciousness; / By merely being remembered once, it gives the supreme abode.
The two jewels of mantras, the installation, effort, taking refuge: / The mantra 'Lakṣmīnārāyaṇa' is the bestower of all fruits.
Know the names of the jewel of mantras in succession. / By its mere recitation I am perpetually pleased.
Be he of noble birth or an ascetic, one who has mastered the Vedas and Vedāṅgas, / Or devoted to sacrifices and gifts, one who serves all sacred places,
Observant of vows, truthful, a mendicant, or even a man of wisdom: / [If] he is not qualified for the mantra, one should avoid him with effort.
Brāhmaṇas, kṣatriyas, vaiśyas, women, śūdras, and also others— / they are all eligible for it, if only they are devoted to me.
And to those who have no other refuge, and likewise to those who serve no other, / and to those who practice no other means, this supreme mantra should be taught.
To the afflicted, it yields fruit quickly even when recited just once; / and even for arrogant creatures, it averts another embodiment.
Whether afflicted, seeking knowledge, desiring wealth, or a wise sage, O Prajāpati, / if he takes refuge in me once, he then obtains his desires.
It should not be spoken to one who is uninitiated, nor to one who lacks devotion, nor to the arrogant, / nor to a materialist, nor to the greedy, nor to one averse to faith,
Nor should it be spoken to one who does not serve, nor to one who has not dwelt [as a pupil] for a full year. / But to one freed from desire and anger, abandoned by deceit and greed,
And who serves me through unwavering bhakti-yoga, / to him the peerless jewel of mantras must be declared according to rule.
Rules of place and time, examination of friendly and hostile letters, / nyāsa, mudrās, and the like, together with its preliminary rites,
Having the body marked with my discus, the worship of what is mine, / renunciation of all actions unto me, having no other refuge than me,
Surrendering all results unto me, preceded by great trust, / effort with no other means, and the sense of one's own utter destitution,
Avoiding conversation with non-Vaiṣṇavas, their greeting, and the like, / and [avoiding] greeting and worship of other deities—
Rules such as these are proclaimed for one who has taken refuge. / To one endowed with such virtues, the supreme mantra must be spoken.
I, Nārāyaṇa, the eternal Viṣṇu, am its seer; / and together with Śrī, I, the ocean of affection, am its deity.
Lord of all the worlds, glorious, virtuous, and blessed, / omniscient, all-powerful, ever fulfilled of purpose,
All-pervading, friend to all, and an ocean of the nectar of grace— / I, glorious Nārāyaṇa, am declared to be the deity.
The metre is the divine Gāyatrī, consisting of twenty-five syllables. / One should assign the six limbs with two, seven, six, three, five, and two [syllables].
One should meditate upon me, together with the inseparable Lakṣmī, in my universal form, / bearing the discus, conch, mace, and lotus in hand, of divine form.

Pure and self-controlled, one should worship [me] together with Śrī seated on my left lap, / with this jewel of mantras, through offerings of fragrant paste and flowers; / even when worshipped only once, I am well pleased, O Prajāpati.
Brahmā said: / You have properly spoken this supreme secret, O Lord, / and the power of this jewel of mantras, which grants all perfections to mortals.
You are the father of all worlds, you are the mother, and the guru; / you are the master, friend, brother, destiny, refuge, and benefactor.
Indeed, O Lord of gods, I am your servant, disciple, and friend; / therefore, O ocean of compassion, you have declared this supreme [secret] to me.
Now declare fully, according to rule and in its entirety, / the initiation of this jewel of mantras, desiring the welfare of the worlds.
The Blessed Lord said: / Listen, my child, I shall declare the supreme rule for mantra initiation. / One should first seek shelter in a preceptor to attain refuge in me.
The preceptor must be accomplished in the Vedas, devoted to Viṣṇu, free from envy, / knowing the mantra, devoted to the mantra, ever sheltered by the mantra, pure,
Belonging to a true tradition, expert in the knowledge of Brahman, / having no other means and having no other purpose,
A brāhmaṇa, free from passion, devoid of anger and greed, / a director in good conduct, a seeker of liberation, and knower of the Supreme Self.
An ācārya endowed with these and other virtues is a friend to all; / he who instructs in proper conduct (ācāra) is called an ācārya.
He who is dependent on the preceptor, if instructed in good conduct, / and is steady in obedience, is called a disciple by the virtuous.
To a disciple endowed with such characteristics and possessing all good qualities, / [the preceptor] should teach the peerless jewel of mantras according to rule.
On the twelfth lunar day, or on Śravaṇa, or on some Vaiṣṇava day, / the good preceptor, being well pleased, should perform initiation there.
One should have Sudarśana and Pāñcajanya made of gold, / or of silver, or of copper, or of bronze.
Having bathed them with the pure five nectars, one should worship them before me; / one should worship them with incense, flowers, and the rest according to rule with their mantras.
There the preceptor, the best of the twice-born, should establish the fire / according to the rite prescribed in his own Gṛhyasūtra and then offer clarified butter with the mantra.
He should make offerings with the jewel of mantras one thousand and eight times, / or one hundred and eight times, and likewise with other auspicious Vaiṣṇava mantras.
With mantras such as the Puruṣasūkta, he should offer clarified butter and milk pudding; / and into that fire the best of the twice-born should place the discus and conch.
He should offer clarified butter twenty times with the six-syllable mantra; / then taking the heated discus with the mantra, the guru,
And likewise with the conch, should brand the right and left arms; / then, concluding the remainder of the oblation, he should perform worship again.
Then, taking a water pot filled with pure water, / consecrating it with the mantra, he should sprinkle it upon his head.
To the disciple, wearing white garments, properly purified by sipping water, endowed with humility, / and bearing the upright forehead mark (ūrdhvapuṇḍra), the guru should teach the mantra.
The meaning of the mantra should be explained, and especially the conduct. / Having received the mantra, he should worship the preceptor with ornaments and other gifts.
