6.223.m:
Whoever studies the mantra from a Vaiṣṇava guru according to this rule, / he then reaches the realm of Viṣṇu, not otherwise, O best of gods.

Nārada said: / Having spoken thus to the Creator, Hari, the god of gods, the Father, / having marked him with his discus, personally gave him the mantra.
Lord of all worlds, the god Brahmā, my father and lord, / also gave that mantra to me according to rule, O best of sages.
Therefore, O best of sages, bearing the Sudarśana [mark], / go for refuge to the pair of Nārāyaṇa's feet, O twice-born!
Vasiṣṭha said: / Having been addressed thus by the divine sage Nārada, all the sages, / qualified for the dual [mantra], all went to the supreme abode of Viṣṇu.
Therefore you too, royal sage, desiring union with Viṣṇu, / bearing Sudarśana according to the rule of the path of initiation,
Go to that pair of Nārāyaṇa's feet alone for refuge; / he is the lord of all worlds, Brahmā manifest, the lord of the three worlds.
Declared the supreme mantra to me and also to Nārada. / Nārada imparted the mantra, surrender (prapatti) and taking refuge,
To the great sages headed by Śaunaka who dwell in the Naimiṣa forest. / This is the most secret mystery, O king, which the great sages do not know;
The gods do not know it, nor do the siddhas, sādhyas, and dānavas. / Parāśara, the son of Śakti, was also given the mantra by me.
This supreme secret is the dual [mantra] of Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa; / O king, I will declare to you also surrender and taking refuge.
There is no mantra higher than the Dvaya mantra; I tell you the truth: / there is no dharma higher than this in all the worlds.
True, true, again true, it was declared by Brahmā of old: / there is no god higher than Nārāyaṇa who bestows liberation upon mortals.
Service to him alone yields liberation, cutting away all karma.

6.224.m: Dilīpa said: / Venerable one, declare everything full of the nectar of devotion to Hari; / as I listen to devotion to Viṣṇu, which brings happiness, I am never satiated.
For human beings who are continually scorched / by the fires of the great blazes of the three afflictions, O best of sages, / except for the ocean of the nectar of devotion to Viṣṇu,

what other refuge is there in the terrifying forest of worldly existence? / Therefore tell me in detail, O great sage, the varieties of devotion / to the Supreme Self, which are constantly practiced by sages.
Vasiṣṭha said: / You ask well, O king of kings, concerning the rescue of men from worldly existence, / and about devotion to Vaikuṇṭha, the supreme Lord, which brings eternal happiness.
This very great question, in ancient times on the peak of Kailāsa, / the goddess Girijā asked Śaṅkara, who is worshiped by all the worlds.
Pārvatī said: / O God of gods, Great God, destroyer of Tripura, Lord of the gods, / explain to me devotion to Viṣṇu, which grants liberation to all embodied beings,
and the various forms of the deity to be worshipped, the mantras, and his rituals of worship, / as well as the true nature of that Viṣṇu, his divine manifestations, his qualities, and so forth;
the nature of his realm, which having attained one does not return; / by means of which the Blessed Lord Hari performs creation, maintenance, and dissolution;
that supreme abode of Hari, which having reached they do not return; / and by which ritual action or practice that supreme state
is attained even by sinful men whose minds are attached to sensory objects. / Out of affection for me, tell me everything in detail, without omission.
Vasiṣṭha said: / Thus questioned by the Great Goddess, Hara, the destroyer of Tripura, / then spoke with supreme affection, having bowed to Janārdana.
Rudra said: / Well said, well said, O Great Goddess, wishing welfare to all the worlds! / You ask me well, O goddess, about the supreme glory of the Lord of Śrī.
You are fortunate, you have performed merit, you are devoted to Viṣṇu, O Pārvatī! / I am always delighted with you, O auspicious one, because of your virtuous conduct, beauty, and good qualities.
Now I shall tell you, O Girijā, of the supreme devotion to the Lord, / the rule of his mantras, and the true nature of that wielder of the Śārṅga bow.
The ultimate Reality is Nārāyaṇa, Viṣṇu, eternal Vāsudeva, / the Supreme Self, the Supreme Brahman, the Supreme Light, higher than the highest,

6.224.s:
acyutaḥ puruṣaḥkṛṣṇaḥ śāśvataḥ śivaīśvaraḥ
nityaḥ sarvagataḥ sthāṇūrudrassākṣīprajāpatiḥ
6.224.d:
अच्युतः पुरुषःकृष्णः शाश्वतः शिवईश्वरः
नित्यः सर्वगतः स्थाणूरुद्रस्साक्षीप्रजापतिः
6.224.m: Acyuta, the Puruṣa, Kṛṣṇa, the everlasting, Śiva, the Lord, / the eternal, the all-pervading, the immovable, Rudra, the witness, Prajāpati,
the sacrifice, the Lord of sacrifice, directly the Lord of Brahman itself, / Hiraṇyagarbha, the Sun, the maker of the world, the supporter of the world, the all-pervading sovereign,
the Blessed Lord designated by the syllable 'A', the Lord and husband of Śrī, Bhū, and Nīlā, / and the ruler of immortality, which grows beyond through food,
having a thousand heads, the Soul of the universe, thousand-eyed, thousand-footed; / he, having pervaded the earth on all sides, stood ten fingers beyond it,
infinite, the Lord of Śrī, Rāma, bearer of qualities, devoid of qualities, great, / the Lord of all the worlds, glorious, omniscient, facing everywhere.
Of that foremost of the worlds, the Lord of the universe, O Pārvatī, / of Vāsudeva, as much of his majesty as can be spoken, that I shall declare to you.
It is impossible even for me, along with Brahmā and the deities, to declare / that meaning of all the Upaniṣads, fully ascertained in the Vedānta.
Hear also the varieties of his worship, which I speak of distinctly: / the first, said to belong to a Vaiṣṇava, is the branding of the conch and discus of Hari,
and the wearing of the upright marks, the reception of his mantras, / worship, recitation, meditation, and remembering his names,
praising, hearing, bowing, serving his feet, / honoring the water that washed his feet, eating food offered to him,
service to his devotees, steadfast observance of the Dvādaśī vow, / and planting the tulasī plant for Viṣṇu, the God of gods, who bears the Śārṅga bow.
Devotion is spoken of as sixteenfold for release from the bondage of worldly existence. / For all the gods, and even for me, the Supreme Puruṣa,
Hari, is always to be worshiped, especially by brāhmaṇas; / therefore, a brāhmaṇa should always worship Hari according to the prescribed rules.
Marked with his emblems, he attains the abode of the Lord of Śrī without doubt. / A brāhmaṇa should make the brand of the conch and discus on the roots of his arms,
heated in sacrificial fire, for the eradication of all sins: / either the discus, or the conch and discus, or the five weapons.
Only having worn them according to rule should he undertake Vedic rites. / Having indeed borne on the roots of his arms what is fire-heated and pure,
abandoning the terrible city of Yama, he goes to the supreme abode of Viṣṇu. / But one who worships Keśava without the emblem of the discus,
all of that—worship, mantras, recitation, and so forth—comes to no fruition. / Having marked the roots of his arms with the discus heated in fire,
a brāhmaṇa who recites the mantra attains liberation from worldly existence. / Having worn the Sudarśana heated in fire, the best of the twice-born,
having initiated [a student] according to rule, should then employ him in rituals. / He who feeds in a ancestral rite one who is devoid of Viṣṇu's discus,
all of that becomes useless, and his ancestors depart disappointed. / One should honor a vipra who is marked with Viṣṇu's discus in an ancestral rite;
one who is devoid of Viṣṇu's discus, however, he should carefully avoid. / One should indeed give cows, land, gold, and other gifts to one whose arms are marked with the discus;
whatever is given to one devoid of the discus is indeed given to an Asura. / Those marked on the roots of their arms with the discus heated in fire,
freed from all sins, go to the supreme abode of Viṣṇu. / One whose body is marked with the discus heated in the sacrificial fire,
sacred bathing places and sacrifices are attained by him; of this there is no doubt. / Without wearing the discus according to rule, a brāhmaṇa becomes vulgar;
one should not eat anything of his, even if he has performed a thousand sacrifices. / A brāhmaṇa who has not worn the discus according to rule finds knowledge difficult to obtain;
reviled in all the worlds, he falls from brāhmaṇahood. / Just as Lord Hari, who bears the conch and discus, is to be worshiped by souls,
even so a vipra marked with the discus and other signs is to be worshiped by all. / Even if he knows all the Vedas, even if he is skilled in all the treatises,
without wearing the discus according to rule, a brāhmaṇa becomes fallen. / One who is devoid of the upright mark, however, and abandoned by the conch and discus—
having mounted him upon a donkey, one should cast him outside of one's own town. / Vāsudeva Janārdana is untouched by material nature;
just so, O goddess, is a brāhmaṇa marked with Viṣṇu's discus. / Therefore, the heated discus and conch of Hari, which burn the flood of sins
arising from contact with material nature, he should wear on the roots of his arms. / For women and śūdras, they are always to be worn made with fragrant sandalwood paste;
one should draw the discus on the root of the arm, but for a brāhmaṇa it must be heated. / One should perform the branding of a brāhmaṇa according to the rite only with what is heated,
for the accomplishment of Vedic and traditional duties, for the accomplishment of mantras, / and for entitlement to the worship of Hari, the discus is to be worn according to rule.
For the accomplishment of the state of a Vaiṣṇava, and for the accomplishment of knowledge, / having offered the oblation according to rule, one should brand oneself with the discus and conch.
A brāhmaṇa should not brand his body with any emblems other than Hari's marks, / nor with any emblems of Hari other than the conch, discus, mace, sword, and the Śārṅga bow.
One should brand the body with the mark [of Hari]; one branded with anything else is not entitled to rites. / One should avoid from afar a brahmin who does not bear the discus.
One should not look upon a non-Vaiṣṇava brahmin in this world any more than upon an outcaste dog-cooker; / even an outcaste who is a Vaiṣṇava purifies the three worlds.
Therefore, O fair-faced woman, the discus must be borne according to rule by brahmins, / both for the success of mantras and for the attainment of knowledge and liberation.
Those marked with Viṣṇu's discus are exalted, non-ordinary beings; / but brahmins devoid of Viṣṇu's discus are regarded as ordinary, worldly folk.
For brahmins dwelling in all stages of life, especially, / the Vaiṣṇava discus is to be borne according to rule, indeed by the command of the Veda.
On the right arm the brahmin should bear Sudarśana, / and on the left the conch: so know the knowers of Brahman.
Thus the bearing of the discus and other [weapons] is taught in the Mahopaniṣad, / and likewise it is taught in the Sāman, the Yajus, and the Ṛc, O fair-faced woman:
"O Viṣṇu, the lords of men, to cross the ocean of rebirth, bear upon the root of their two arms / your pure lotus and discus; others, ancient ones, offer [their] bodies as signs belonging to you."
"The pure, extensive, ancient foot consists of holy speech; / branded by that discus, they cross the ocean of sin."
"The purifier belonging to Brahmaṇaspati always pervades the universe of Hari; / those whose bodies are not heated by it do not reach the supreme abode."
"Those whose bodies are heated by it proceed to the supreme abode; / the pure foot and rim is the Sudarśana discus of Hari,"
"thousand-spoked, destroyer of the mundane, door to the world, of immense energy." / Learn from me the synonyms of Viṣṇu's discus:
"Purify us through the pure [discus] heated by fire, having the nature of Brahman; / purify us, O Agni, with that purifier of yours which is like a flame;"
"with which purifier the gods continually purify themselves, / with that thousand-streamed [purifier] may the purifying verses cleanse me;"
"the purifier of Prajāpati is hundred-extended and golden; / we, knowers of Brahman, purify the purified Brahman with it;"
"the rimmed, ageless discus is the eye of this Great Soul; / when this is borne, indeed, the gods attained a greatly elevated state."
Therefore the weapons—the conch, discus, and others—must be borne according to rule, / particularly by brahmins, and especially by Vaiṣṇavas.

The noble soul who bears the vertical mark, who has taken up the discus, and contemplates the abode of Viṣṇu, / residing in the heart always through tone and mantra, goes with completely pure mind beyond the highest.

Those with garlands of tulasī and lotus seeds adorning their necks, whose arm-roots are marked with conch and discus, / on whose forehead-slabs the vertical mark shines—those Vaiṣṇavas swiftly purify the world.
"Those who are guardians, yet do not properly bear on their arm / the wide-extended purifier of the Lord of Heaven, those beings surely grieve."
"Those who promptly bear on their arm the stable discus according to rule, / abide by their splendor in your abode in the supreme firmament."

Marked at the root of the two arms with the purifier heated in sacrificial fire, / having crossed the great ocean of existence, one goes pure to the supreme world of the supreme Lord, Hari, the Supreme Self.
One should mark oneself at the root of the arms with the heated discus and other [weapons]; / one should also mark one's wife, children, servants, cattle, and the rest.
Thus all the Vedas declare, O fair-faced lady; / in that very manner it is also told in the legendary histories and Purāṇas.
A Vaiṣṇava is spoken of as twofold: external and internal. / External is by the conch, discus, and other marks; internal is freedom from passion.
The harmony of the external and the internal is declared to be the true Vaiṣṇava state; / therefore, the sign of the discus and the rest is recognized as the first mark of a Vaiṣṇava.
The internal consists of perception of the Self, free from the blemishes of desire and the like, / compassion for all beings, tranquility, freedom from greed toward sense objects,
non-attachment to sons, wife, and the like, delight in the practice of yoga, / and attendance upon the Supreme Lord through single-minded devotional yoga.
Therefore, the branding of the weapons such as the discus is considered the mark of a Vaiṣṇava; / without the signs such as the discus, one cannot attain the state of a Vaiṣṇava.

6.225.m: Śaṃkara said: / I shall declare the glorification of the vertical mark, O woman of auspicious sight; / by merely wearing it, an excellent twice-born is freed from the bondage of worldly existence.
In the spacious, captivating center of the vertical mark / sits Janārdana, the God of gods, together with Lakṣmī.
Therefore, on whosever body the vertical mark is borne, / that person's body is the pure, auspicious temple of the Lord.
A Vaiṣṇava who bears the vertical mark made of white clay / has bathed in all holy places and is consecrated in all sacrifices.
A brahmin bearing the vertical mark is revered in all worlds; / mounting an excellent celestial chariot, he goes to the supreme abode of Viṣṇu.
An excellent twice-born should wear the vertical mark at the three junctures of the day, / for the purification of all sins and to obtain the fruit of sacrificial and charitable works.
Seeing one who bears the vertical mark, one is released from all sins; / or bowing to him with devotion, one obtains the fruit of all gifts.
Whoever feeds a brahmin bearing the vertical mark at an ancestral rite— / his ancestors are satisfied for ten million cosmic cycles, without a doubt.
He who, bearing the vertical mark, performs an ancestral rite, O fair-faced woman, / obtains the fruit of an ancestral rite at Gayā for a thousand tens of millions of cosmic cycles.
Whatever sacrifice, gift, practice of austerity, silent recitation, oblation, and the like / one bearing the vertical mark performs, his merit is infinite.
Whatever rite one devoid of the vertical mark performs, / all his sacrificial and charitable works become fruitless, without a doubt.
That body of men which is devoid of the vertical mark / should not be looked upon at all; it is like a cremation ground.
If one devoid of the vertical mark performs the twilight ritual and other rites, / it is all taken away by rākṣasas, and he falls into hell.
A twice-born faithful to the Veda should bear the vertical mark with white clay; / a wise man should never wear it horizontally, even in times of distress.
For brahmins there should be the vertical mark; for a king, a circular mark; / for vaiśyas, a stripe shape; and for śūdras, indeed, the triple horizontal mark.
The vertical mark should be made with clay, the circular mark with musk, / the stripe shape with fragrant paste, and the triple horizontal mark with ash alone.
The vertical mark is never prohibited for anyone; / even a kṣatriya and the rest may wear it if he becomes a devotee of Viṣṇu.
Brahmins should never wear a horizontal stripe or the like, / nor worship any other than Nārāyaṇa, the Supreme Lord.
If a well-born, learned brahmin becomes a wearer of ash, / one should shun him, O goddess, like a vessel tainted with liquor.
The triple horizontal mark is the rule for those equal to śūdras and for śūdras; / from wearing the triple horizontal mark, a brahmin falls from caste, without a doubt.
Single-minded devotees, fortunate and intent on the welfare of all beings, / should make the sectarian mark with a central space, shaped like Hari's foot.
One should fashion an upright mark in the shape of Hari's foot according to rule, / furnished with a space in the middle; for that indeed is Hari's temple.
One should construct an upright mark that is straight, pleasing, well-flanked, most charming, / staff-shaped, full of beauty, with a space in the middle.
Therefore, a mark with a space, staff-shaped and very beautiful, / must always be applied by brahmins and by women, O auspicious-looking lady.
For in the middle of the upright mark, which is broad and very lovely, / seated within the intervening space, resides Hari together with Śrī.
The vile twice-born who makes an upright mark without an intervening space / drives away both Viṣṇu and Śrī residing therein.
Those vile twice-born who make an upright mark without a gap, / on their forehead there is continually a dog's foot, without doubt.
Therefore, a mark provided with a gap, along with turmeric, endowed with auspiciousness, / a brahmin should constantly wear for the attainment of Hari's world.
Taking clay from the lake on the Veṅkaṭa mountain with supreme devotion, / one should apply upright marks for the attainment of union with Hari.
A devoted person, taking clay from the root of a sacred tulasī of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, / should apply upright marks; Hari is pleased by that.
Likewise in Dvāravatī, auspicious and charming, and in the lake of Vāsudeva— / taking the delightful clay produced there, the best of the twice-born
should wear upright marks to obtain the fruit of all desires. / Taking with supreme devotion the clay produced on the bank of the Gaṅgā,
one who has thus applied upright marks obtains the fruit of all sacrifices. / Sandalwood, turmeric, and likewise ash produced from an Agnihotra,
are declared to bring all under control through the wearing of an upright mark. / Wherever there is a holy field of Hari, from there indeed one should fetch clay:
on a mountain summit, on a riverbank, at the root of a bilva tree, at a body of water, / on the seashore, and at an anthill, especially in a field of Hari,
where the bath-water of Viṣṇu flows perpetually— / for the sake of wearing the marks, one should take the clay there.
In Śrīraṅga, on the Veṅkaṭa mountain, at Śrīkūrma, in auspicious Dvārakā, / in Prayāga, on the Narasiṃha mountain, at Vārāha, and in a tulasī grove,
having taken clay with devotion along with water from Viṣṇu's feet, / and having applied the marks on the limbs, one attains union with Viṣṇu.
Whatever [clay] fortunate Vaiṣṇavas wear, / that clay indeed should be taken for wearing the upright mark.
Black is said to produce peace, red to bring under control; / yellow they declare to bring prosperity, and white is auspicious, producing liberation.
Round, horizontal, unbroken, short, excessively long, thin, / crooked, misshapen, tied at the top, severed at the root, misplaced,
inauspicious, rough, smeared, and made without fingers, / foul-smelling, and repulsive: they declare such a mark to be useless.
Starting from the root of the nose, one should draw it with clay up to the forehead; / beginning between the eyebrows, one should fashion an intervening space.
The space in between should be two finger-breadths, and the two sides should measure one finger-breadth; / with white clay one should draw an upright, auspicious puṇḍra mark.
One should meditate on Keśava on the forehead, then on Nārāyaṇa on the belly, / on Mādhava on the chest, and on Govinda at the hollow of the throat;
on Viṣṇu on the right side of the abdomen, and on Madhusūdana on the [right] arm; / on Trivikrama at the [right side of the] neck, and on Vāmana on the left side;
on Śrīdhara on the left arm, and on Hṛṣīkeśa at the [left side of the] neck; / on Padmanābha on the back, and one should place Dāmodara on the sacrum;
and on Vāsudeva on the head with the water used to wash it off. / On the forehead, on the pair of arms, on the two [sides of the] back, and at the hollow of the throat,
one should wear an upright mark measuring four finger-breadths. / On the abdomen and its flanks, it is declared to be ten finger-breadths long.
On the arms and on the chest, the mark is proclaimed to be eight finger-breadths. / In this way, a brahmin should constantly wear twelve marks.
Having meditated on the respective forms with the mantra, he should wear those respective marks; / in all the intervening spaces, he should apply turmeric for Śrī.
Four marks are declared for kings; two are remembered for the vaiśyas; / a single mark is prescribed for women and for śūdras.
One should wear four marks: on the forehead, on the chest, and on the two arms. / Two are on the forehead and on the chest, but one is prescribed on the forehead.
The upright mark on the forehead is remembered as the first for all; / indeed, wearing them in order beginning from the forehead is prescribed.
In the case of four marks, one should maintain the forms beginning with Vāsudeva; / in the case of two, Govinda and Kṛṣṇa; but with one, one should maintain Nārāyaṇa.
In this way the rule of the marks has been declared by me for all, O Mountain-born Lady. / Resembling an aśvattha leaf, shaped like a bamboo leaf,
and resembling a lotus bud—this triad is remembered as enchanting. / A pure, great devotee of the Lord [wears] a mark shaped like Hari's foot;
or, O goddess, one should wear an upright mark shaped like a staff. / Those whose upper arms are marked with the Sudarśana, and whose whole bodies are marked with upright marks,
wearing garlands and lotus-seed beads, being entirely pure, protect the worlds from the contact of the flood of sins.

Thus ends the two hundred and twenty-fifth chapter, named the Glorification of the Ūrdhvapuṇḍra, in the dialogue between Umā and Maheśvara, in the Uttarakhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Purāṇa, the collection of fifty-five thousand [verses].

6.226.m: Śaṃkara said: / Whether in assignment or in worship, an exclusive devotee should resort to the mantra. / Through a mantra taught by a non-Vaiṣṇava, there is no supreme goal.
If the pair of supreme mantras was previously taught by a non-Vaiṣṇava, / one should properly receive it again according to rule from a Vaiṣṇava guru.
Though he has studied a thousand Vedic branches, or has been initiated in all sacrifices, / or has been born into a great family, a non-Vaiṣṇava cannot be a guru.
He, however, who as a Vaiṣṇava properly teaches the two mantras, / is to be known as the ācārya who severs the bonds of worldly existence.
Having resorted to the ācārya, the twice-born should then serve him for a year; / having known his conduct, the guru should instruct him in the mantra.
Having performed the purificatory rites such as branding, he should utter the mantra afterward. / The guru, having performed the branding, the mark, and the naming according to rule,
should afterward instruct the pure-minded disciple in the mantra. / Heated by the discus according to rule—this is called branding.
The upright mark is likewise declared, and the name is said to be Vaiṣṇava. / Then the guru should instruct the disciple in the mantra according to rule:
the mantra of assignment, the eight-syllable mantra, or another Vaiṣṇava formula. / Assignment itself is the highest here for Vaiṣṇavas, O fair-faced lady;
therefore, assignment alone is declared here to be superior for them. / A brahmin who is devoted to the wisdom of assignment is said to be the best.
There is no mantra higher than assignment; I tell you the truth. / Assignment is the Dvaya, surrender; understand from me by synonym.
Preceded by instruction in the Dvaya, one should perform every religious act. / One who is not qualified for the Dvaya is not fit for any religious acts.
Therefore, having studied the Dvaya itself, the best of the twice-born should then / properly practice the unexcelled, glorious eight-syllable mantra.
The eight-syllable mantra is taught precisely through the inclusion of the praṇava; / for the wise say that the natural praṇava is the beginning and the end of the mantra.
The praṇava does not belong inherently to all other mantras; / but at the beginning of all mantras, one should join the auspicious praṇava.
The syllable [oṃ] is the praṇava, Brahman, the leader among all mantras; / one should apply it at the beginning everywhere among mantras, O fair-faced woman.
By its nature, the praṇava is established in that root mantra: / first the single syllable *om*, then the two-syllable *namas*,
then *nārāyaṇāya*, five syllables in regular succession; / thus the eight-syllable mantra, which accomplishes all ends, should be understood.
Dispelling all sorrow, glorious, embodying all mantras, auspicious; / its seer is Nārāyaṇa, and its deity is the Lord of Śrī.
Its meter is the goddess Gāyatrī; the praṇava is called its seed; / the goddess Śrī, ever-inseparable, is called the power of the mantra.
The first word is called *oṅkāra*, the second *namas*; / the third is declared as *nārāyaṇāya*—three words are thus spoken.
The letter *a*, then *u*, and after that *m*: / the praṇava, the abode of Brahman, is said to consist of the three Vedas.
By the letter *a*, Viṣṇu is denoted, and Śrī is denoted by the letter *u*; / but the letter *m* is proclaimed as their servant, the twenty-fifth principle.
That nature of Vāsudeva is spoken of by the wise through the letter *a*; / through the letter *u*, the form of the goddess Śrī is spoken of by sages.
Through the letter *m*, the individual soul is spoken of, proclaimed as the twenty-fifth person; / the elements are signified by the *ka*-class, and the sense organs by the *ca*-class;
knowledge and the organs of action by the *ṭa*-class and the *ta*-class; / the mind is declared by the letter *pa*, and egoism by the letter *pha*;
by the letter *ba* the intellect is spoken of, and by *bha* primordial matter; / and the self is the letter *ma*, proclaimed as the twenty-fifth.
Different from the body, senses, mind, breath, and the rest, having no other means, / this conscious being, named by the letter *ma*, is a subordinate accessory to the Lord.
In this way, some state that the letter *u* has an exclusive sense [“only”]; / on that view as well, the principle of Śrī is expressed through the letter *va*.
Just as radiance belongs to the sun, eternally inseparable from it, / so by the letter 'A' is Viṣṇu designated, the ocean of auspicious qualities,

the Lord of Śrī, the sovereign whole of all individual souls, the seed of the universe, the Supreme Person, / the maker of the universe, the sustainer of the universe, the Lord, the friend of all worlds.
The eternal mistress of the worlds, who never departs from Viṣṇu, / the mother of the entire universe, the delightful consort of Viṣṇu,
Śrī, the foundation of the world, is designated here by the letter 'U'. / By the letter 'M', the knower of the field, their servant, is declared by the wise.

He is the resting place of knowledge, endowed with the attribute of knowledge, conscious, beyond material nature, / neither insentient nor subject to modification, possessing a uniform intrinsic nature,
atomic, eternal, pervading by nature, consisting of consciousness and bliss, / the sense of the word 'I', imperishable, the embodied soul, distinct in form, everlasting,
incombustible, uncleavable, not to be moistened, undriable, and imperishable. / Endowed with such qualities as these, he is truly subordinate to the Supreme.
By the letter 'M' is designated the living soul, the knower of the field, ever dependent on another, / being a servant of Hari alone, and never of anyone else.
Thus his state of servanthood alone is established as the middle meaning. / In this way the meaning of the Praṇava, which should be known, has been spoken by me, O sinless one.
The exposition of the meaning of the Praṇava is indeed [completed] by the remainder of the mantra, O auspicious lady: / For him who is a servant of the Supreme, no independence exists in this world.
Therefore, one should turn away the great egoism with the mind. / Even whatever action is done with the idea of one's own means is forbidden.
The letter 'M' is the notion of 'I', and the letter 'N' is its negation. / Therefore, the cessation of his egoism comes about through the mind alone.
Through the mind all accomplishment is attained; otherwise one would meet destruction. / Anything accompanied by 'namas' [prostration/negation of 'mine']—that is spoken of [as abandoning] egoism.
For one conjoined with egoism, not the slightest happiness exists; / one whose self is deluded by egoism sinks into blinding darkness.
Therefore, by the 'namas' here, independence is forbidden; / he is entirely dependent on the Lord, and his life depends on Him.
Therefore, the agency of adopting means does not belong to the conscious soul; / by the will of the Lord alone does the moving and unmoving world proceed in its own way.
Therefore, one should abandon completely all reliance upon one's own capability; / for through the power of the Lord, nothing is unobtainable to him.
Having placed one's burden on Him, the Lord of Śrī, one should perform that duty alone: / 'The Supreme Self, Hari, is my master, and I am ever His property.
I am to be employed according to the will of that very Lord of the self.' / In this way, the arrogance of 'I-ness' and 'my-ness' is abandoned through the mind.
The thought of 'I' regarding bodies is the root of worldly existence and the bondage of karma; / therefore, the wise person should abandon the great egoism with the mind.
Now I shall speak of the word 'Nārāyaṇa', O auspicious daughter of the mountain: / 'Nārāḥ' are the multitudes of souls; that Person is their goal.
And they are His abode; therefore He is remembered as Nārāyaṇa. / For every conscious and non-conscious entity in the world that is heard or seen—
He who stands eternally pervading all that is remembered as Nārāyaṇa. / Moreover, 'nārāḥ' are proclaimed as the multitudes of all embodied souls;
He is their goal and support; therefore He is remembered as Nārāyaṇa. / The wise know that the principles born of Nara are called 'nārāḥ';
and they are His abode, so by that He is remembered as Nārāyaṇa. / By whom the entire universe, having been swallowed at the end of a cosmic age, is sustained,
and by whom it is created again—He indeed is remembered as Nārāyaṇa. / The entire universe of moving and unmoving beings is designated as 'nāra';
He in whom is its dwelling and refuge—by that He is remembered as Nārāyaṇa. / 'Nāra' is the collection of men; He is their abode and refuge;
therefore is He eternally proclaimed as Nārāyaṇa by the sages. / Whence the worlds arise, like large foam upon the great ocean,
and into whom they dissolve again, therefore is He remembered as Nārāyaṇa. / He who is eternal in the eternal realm, enjoying the sole enjoyment of the eternally liberated,

6.226.s:
īśaḥ sarvasyajagataḥ savainārāyaṇaḥ smṛtaḥ
nārāyaṇaḥ paraṃbrahmatatvaṃnārāyaṇaḥ param
6.226.d:
ईशः सर्वस्यजगतः सवैनारायणः स्मृतः
नारायणः परंब्रह्मतत्वंनारायणः परम्
6.226.m: the Lord of the entire universe—He indeed is remembered as Nārāyaṇa. / Nārāyaṇa is the Supreme Brahman; Nārāyaṇa is the Supreme Reality.
And whatever is seen or heard in this world, / having pervaded all that inside and outside, Nārāyaṇa stands.
The Person whose sins are dispelled, dwelling within all beings, / divine, one, ever eternal, is Hari, Nārāyaṇa, Acyuta.
He who is the seer and the object to be seen, the hearer and the object to be heard, / the toucher and the object to be touched, the meditator and the object to be meditated upon,
the speaker and what is to be spoken, the knower and what is to be known, the universe of conscious and non-conscious— / all that is Hari, the Lord of Śrī, declared as Nārāyaṇa.
The Person has a thousand heads, a thousand eyes, a thousand feet; / having pervaded the worlds on every side, He stood ten fingers' breadth beyond.
Whatever has been and whatever is to be—all that is Nārāyaṇa, Hari; / and He is the lord of immortality, since [He became] the cosmic Person by food.
He alone is the Person, Viṣṇu, Vāsudeva, Acyuta, Hari, / full of gold, the blessed Lord, immortal, everlasting, auspicious [Śiva],
the master of the entire universe, the Lord and master of all worlds, / Hiraṇyagarbha, the Sun, the Infinite, that Great Lord.
The word 'Bhagavān' as well as 'Puruṣa' / applies without limitation to Vāsudeva, the Self of all.
He is the Lord, the blessed Lord Viṣṇu, the Supreme Self, the friend of the universe, / the sole ruler of the moving and unmoving, the supreme goal of ascetics.
He who is the sound proclaimed at the beginning of the Vedas and established at the end of the Vedas, / who is beyond that [sound] dissolved into material nature—He is the Great Lord.
He who is the letter 'A' is Viṣṇu, who is Nārāyaṇa, Hari; / He alone is the eternal Person, the Supreme Self, the Great Lord.

Because lordship arises from Him and resides in whoever possesses it, / the word 'Lord' is also spoken of him in that manner by the sages; / indeed, unconditional lordship is established in Vāsudeva alone.
He is proclaimed as the 'Lord of the self' by the eternal Vedic declarations; / therefore, supremacy as the Great Lord is established in Vāsudeva alone.
He is the Lord of the three-quartered realm of glory, and also [of this realm] through His sport; / the twofold realm of glory and lordship belongs to Him alone, the Self of all.
He who is the Lord of Śrī, Bhū, and Nīlā is declared as the Sovereign; / therefore, universal lordship is established in Vāsudeva alone.
He is the Lord of sacrifice, the sacrifice, the enjoyer of sacrifice, the maker of sacrifice, the all-pervading; / He is the enjoyer of sacrifice, the sacrificial Person, the Supreme Lord.
The Lord of sacrifice, the enjoyer of all offerings to gods and ancestors, the imperishable Self, Hari, is the Lord here; / from His presence, all the rākṣasas and all the asuras instantly flee.
He who has assumed the cosmic form, Hari, who has become Janārdana, / gladdens the three worlds; He alone is the Supreme Lord.
With Him as the full oblation, the gods performed the sacrifice; / from that sacrifice were born whatever [beasts] have teeth on both jaws.
From that sacrifice of universal offering, the ṛg-verses and sāman-hymns were born; / from it horses were born, and cows, men, and the rest.
From the body of this Person, who consists entirely of sacrifice, / from Hari, the entire universe arose, both stationary and moving.
His mouth, arms, thighs, and feet are the castes in succession; / from his two feet arose the earth, and from his head the sky.
From His mind the moon was born, and from His eye the sun; / from His mouth came fire and Indra, and from His breath the wind, ever-moving.
From his navel arose Viriñci, the sky, and the entire world, moving and unmoving. / Because everything arose from Viṣṇu, the eternal one,
therefore Viṣṇu, consisting of all things, is spoken of as Nārāyaṇa. / Having thus created the entire universe, Hari swallows it again,
which arose from his own sport, like a web from a spider. / Brahmā, Indra, Rudra, Yama, and Varuṇa—
because he seizes and carries them away, he is therefore called Hari. / When everything becomes a single ocean, that eternal Puruṣa,
having placed the world within his own belly, sleeps beneath the banyan tree of illusion. / Indeed, there alone was the one Viṣṇu, Nārāyaṇa, Acyuta;
there was neither Brahmā nor Rudra, nor gods nor great sages, / neither these heaven and earth, nor moon nor sun,
nor stars nor worlds, nor the great universe enclosed. / Because the entire world was pervaded by him, Hari, O fair one,
and likewise created again at the time of creation, he is remembered as Nārāyaṇa. / In the fourth case [in the mantra], servitude to him is declared, O Pārvatī.
This entire world, beginning with Brahmā, has become his servant. / Having thus known the meaning, one should then employ the mantra.
Without knowing the meaning of the mantra, one never attains accomplishment, / nor enjoyment, nor devotion, nor liberation, O fair-faced one.
